# LiteLLM #24720: latency routing loses concurrent measurements

- Status at capture: open
- Upstream: https://github.com/BerriAI/litellm/issues/24720
- Pinned source: `litellm@8f86c87f8e065343af6e74e0823ab8a8276b9528`

Under concurrent completions, latency-based routing can collapse into a random
selection weighted by deployment count. `async_log_success_event` in
`litellm/router_strategy/lowest_latency.py` reads an entire cached deployment
map, mutates one entry, and writes the whole map back. Concurrent callbacks can
read the same snapshot and overwrite one another, dropping measurements for
other deployments.

    "path": "/knowledge/company/sources/github_public/BerriAI/litellm/issues/24720.json",
    "title": "[Bug]: latency-based-routing degrades to random selection due to lost-update race condition in async_log_success_event",
    "source": "EnterpriseRAG/github_public",
    "content": "{\n  \"artifact_type\": \"issue\",\n  \"author\": \"hassaan-sage\",\n  \"body\": \"### Check for existing issues\\n\\n- [x] I have searched the existing issues and checked that my issue is not a duplicate.\\n\\n### What happened?\\n\\n`latency-based-routing` degrades to random selection weighted by deployment count when handling concurrent requests. With 16 Anthropic keys + 4 OpenAI keys per tier, traffic distributes 80/20 matching the key ratio regardless of actual latency differences between providers (e.g., OpenAI GPT-4.1 at ~583ms vs Anthropic Claude Sonnet at ~1,588ms).\\n\\n**Expected:** Router should favor the faster provider.\\n**Actual:** Traffic distributes proportionally to deployment count \\u2014 identical to `simple-shuffle`.\\n\\n**Root cause:** `async_log_success_event()` in `litellm/router_strategy/lowest_latency.py` performs a non-atomic read-modify-write on a shared cache key (`{model_group}_map`). When concurrent requests complete simultaneously, the last writer overwrites all previous updates, causing latency data to be constantly lost. Deployments with lost data fall back to `latency: [0]` (treated as fastest) and are randomly selected, producing a distribution proportional to deployment count.\\n\\n```python\\n# READ \\u2014 no lock\\nrequest_count_dict = await self.router_cache.async_get_cache(\\n    key=latency_key, local_only=True\\n) or {}\\n\\n# MODIFY \\u2014 in memory\\nrequest_count_dict[id].setdefault(\\\"latency\\\", []).append(final_value)\\n\\n# WRITE \\u2014 overwrites entire dict, no lock\\nawait self.router_cache.async_set_cache(\\n    key=latency_key, value=request_count_dict, ttl=self.routing_args.ttl\\n)\\n```\\n\\nTwo concurrent completions:\\n1. Request A reads `medium_map` \\u2192 `{deploy_1: {latency: [0.5]}}`\\n2. Request B reads `medium_map` \\u2192 same stale snapshot\\n3. Request A writes `{deploy_1: {latency: [0.5, 0.6]}, deploy_5: {latency: [0.3]}}`\\n4. Request B writes `{deploy_1: {latency: [0.5, 0.4]}}` \\u2014 **overwrites A's update, deploy_5 data is lost**\\n\\nSince `_get_available_deployments()` assigns `latency: [0]` to deployments without cached data and randomly shuffles zero-latency ties, the probability of selecting a provider equals its share of total deployments.\\n\\n\\n### Steps to Reproduce\\n\\n1. Configure LiteLLM proxy with `routing_strategy: \\\"latency-based-routing\\\"` and `routing_strategy_args: {ttl: 300, lowest_latency_buffer: 0.1}`\\n2. Add 20 deployments per model group \\u2014 16 Anthropic API keys + 4 OpenAI API keys for the same tier (e.g., `model_name: medium`)\\n3. Send sustained traffic at ~3 req/sec (we used a CronJob sending 160 req/min)\\n4. Collect `REQUEST_START` logs and count which model was selected per request\\n5. Observe traffic distributes ~80% Anthropic / ~20% OpenAI \\u2014 matching the 16:4 key ratio, not actual latency\\n\\n```yaml\\n# config.yaml\\nmodel_list:\\n  - model_name: medium\\n    litellm_params:\\n      model: anthropic/claude-sonnet-4-6\\n      api_key: os.environ/ANTHROPIC_API_KEY_0\\n  # ... repeat for 16 Anthropic keys\\n  - model_name: medium\\n    litellm_params:\\n      model: openai/gpt-4.1\\n      api_key: os.environ/OPENAI_API_KEY_0\\n  # ... repeat for 4 OpenAI keys\\n\\nrouter_settings:\\n  routing_strategy: \\\"latency-based-routing\\\"\\n  routing_strategy_args:\\n    ttl: 300\\n    lowest_latency_buffer: 0.1\\n```\\n\\n```bash\\n# Send test requests and check distribution\\nfor i in $(seq 1 40); do\\n  curl -s -X POST \\\"http://localhost:4000/v1/messages\\\" \\\\\\n    -H \\\"Content-Type: application/json\\\" \\\\\\n    -H \\\"x-api-key: $KEY\\\" \\\\\\n    -H \\\"anthropic-version: 2023-06-01\\\" \\\\\\n    -d '{\\\"model\\\":\\\"medium\\\",\\\"max_tokens\\\":5,\\\"messages\\\":[{\\\"role\\\":\\\"user\\\",\\\"content\\\":\\\"hi\\\"}]}' &\\ndone\\nwait\\n# Result: ~80% claude-sonnet-4-6, ~20% gpt-4.1\\n```\\n\\n\\n### Relevant log output\\n\\n```shell\\nSent 40 concurrent medium-tier requests. Expected latency-based routing to favor OpenAI (583ms avg) over Anthropic (1,588ms avg).\\n\\nActual distribution:\\n  claude-sonnet-4-6: 32 (80.0%)\\n  gpt-4.1:            8 (20.0%)\\n\\nMatches 16:4 Anthropic:OpenAI key ratio exactly \\u2014 no latency differentiation.\\n\\nMeasured provider latencies from same cluster:\\n  medium/anthropic/claude-sonnet-4-6:  3483 samples, avg 1588ms, P50 1622ms, P95 2243ms\\n  medium/openai/gpt-4.1:               875 samples, avg  583ms, P50  514ms, P95  790ms\\n```\\n\\n### What part of LiteLLM is this about?\\n\\nProxy\\n\\n### What LiteLLM version are you on ?\\n\\nv1.82.3\\n\\n### Twitter / LinkedIn details\\n\\n_No response_\",\n  \"changed_files\": [],\n  \"closed_at\": \"\",\n  \"comments_count\": 1,\n  \"commit_summaries\": [],\n  \"content_field_names\": [\n    \"body\",\n    \"conversation\",\n    \"reviews\",\n    \"commit_summaries\",\n    \"changed_files\",\n    \"timeline\"\n  ],\n  \"conversation\": [\n    \"2026-06-04T18:52:44Z Oxygen56: This should be resolved by #29696 \\u2014 per-latency-key locks now serialise the read-modify-write, preventing concurrent completions from overwriting each other's latency data.\"\n  ],\n  \"created_at\": \"2026-03-28T05:12:16Z\",\n  \"dataset_doc_uuid\": \"gh_214a973380c36bbf4ecd3b503c8f246d\",\n  \"draft\": false,\n  \"labels\": [\n    \"bug\",\n    \"llm translation\",\n    \"proxy\"\n  ],\n  \"merged_at\": \"\",\n  \"milestone\": \"\",\n  \"number\": 24720,\n  \"owner\": \"BerriAI\",\n  \"provenance\": [\n    \"GitHub REST and GraphQL API; document.title: [Bug]: latency-based-routing degrades to random selection due to lost-update race condition in async_log_success_event
document.content:
{
  "artifact_type": "issue",
  "author": "hassaan-sage",
  "body": "### Check for existing issues

- [x] I have searched the existing issues and checked that my issue is not a duplicate.

### What happened?

`latency-based-routing` degrades to random selection weighted by deployment count when handling concurrent requests. With 16 Anthropic keys + 4 OpenAI keys per tier, traffic distributes 80/20 matching the key ratio regardless of actual latency differences between providers (e.g., OpenAI GPT-4.1 at ~583ms vs Anthropic Claude Sonnet at ~1,588ms).

**Expected:** Router should favor the faster provider.
**Actual:** Traffic distributes proportionally to deployment count — identical to `simple-shuffle`.

**Root cause:** `async_log_success_event()` in `litellm/router_strategy/lowest_latency.py` performs a non-atomic read-modify-write on a shared cache key (`{model_group}_map`). When concurrent requests complete simultaneously, the last writer overwrites all previous updates, causing latency data to be constantly lost. Deployments with lost data fall back to `latency: [0]` (treated as fastest) and are randomly selected, producing a distribution proportional to deployment count.

```python
# READ — no lock
request_count_dict = await self.router_cache.async_get_cache(
    key=latency_key, local_only=True
) or {}

# MODIFY — in memory
request_count_dict[id].setdefault("latency", []).append(final_value)

# WRITE — overwrites entire dict, no lock
await self.router_cache.async_set_cache(
    key=latency_key, value=request_count_dict, ttl=self.routing_args.ttl
)
```

Two concurrent completions:
1. Request A reads `medium_map` → `{deploy_1: {latency: [0.5]}}`
2. Request B reads `medium_map` → same stale snapshot
3. Request A writes `{deploy_1: {latency: [0.5, 0.6]}, deploy_5: {latency: [0.3]}}`
4. Request B writes `{deploy_1: {latency: [0.5, 0.4]}}` — **overwrites A's update, deploy_5 data is lost**

Since `_get_available_deployments()` assigns `latency: [0]` to deployments without cached data and randomly shuffles zero-latency ties, the probability of selecting a provider equals its share of total deployments.


### Steps to Reproduce

1. Configure LiteLLM proxy with `routing_strategy: "latency-based-routing"` and `routing_strategy_args: {ttl: 300, lowest_latency_buffer: 0.1}`
2. Add 20 deployments per model group — 16 Anthropic API keys + 4 OpenAI API keys for the same tier (e.g., `model_name: medium`)
3. Send sustained traffic at ~3 req/sec (we used a CronJob sending 160 req/min)
4. Collect `REQUEST_START` logs and count which model was selected per request
5. Observe traffic distributes ~80% Anthropic / ~20% OpenAI — matching the 16:4 key ratio, not actual latency

```yaml
# config.yaml
model_list:
  - model_name: medium
    litellm_params:
      model: anthropic/claude-sonnet-4-6
      api_key: os.environ/ANTHROPIC_API_KEY_0
  # ... repeat for 16 Anthropic keys
  - model_name: medium
    litellm_params:
      model: openai/gpt-4.1
      api_key: os.environ/OPENAI_API_KEY_0
  # ... repeat for 4 OpenAI keys

router_settings:
  routing_strategy: "latency-based-routing"
  routing_strategy_args:
    ttl: 300
    lowest_latency_buffer: 0.1
```

```bash
# Send test requests and check distribution
for i in $(seq 1 40); do
  curl -s -X POST "http://localhost:4000/v1/messages" \
    -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
    -H "x-api-key: $KEY" \
    -H "anthropic-version: 2023-06-01" \
    -d '{"model":"medium","max_tokens":5,"messages":[{"role":"user","content":"hi"}]}' &
done
wait
# Result: ~80% claude-sonnet-4-6, ~20% gpt-4.1
```


### Relevant log output

```shell
Sent 40 concurrent medium-tier requests. Expected latency-based routing to favor OpenAI (583ms avg) over Anthropic (1,588ms avg).

Actual distribution:
  claude-sonnet-4-6: 32 (80.0%)
  gpt-4.1:            8 (20.0%)

Matches 16:4 Anthropic:OpenAI key ratio exactly — no latency differentiation.

Measured provider latencies from same cluster:
  medium/anthropic/claude-sonnet-4-6:  3483 samples, avg 1588ms, P50 1622ms, P95 2243ms
  medium/openai/gpt-4.1:               875 samples, avg  583ms, P50  514ms, P95  790ms
```

### What part of LiteLLM is this about?

Proxy

### What LiteLLM version are you on ?

v1.82.3

  "document": {
    "id": "dsid_cd133e76dd62456d9182217e280e2cb3",
    "path": "/knowledge/company/sources/confluence/architecture-and-standards/coding-standards/concurrency-primitives-and-affinity-guidelines-2026.json",
    "title": "concurrency-primitives-and-affinity-guidelines-2026",
    "source": "EnterpriseRAG/confluence",
    "content": "{\n  \"title\": \"concurrency-primitives-and-affinity-guidelines-2026\",\n  \"space\": \"architecture-and-standards/coding-standards\",\n  \"author\": \"Ava Chen\",\n  \"owner_team\": \"engineering\",\n  \"status\": \"published\",\n  \"created_at\": \"2026-01-10\",\n  \"last_updated\": \"2026-03-04\",\n  \"reviewers\": [\n    \"Diego Morales\",\n    \"Priya Nair\"\n  ],\n  \"labels\": [\n    \"concurrency\",\n    \"runtime\",\n    \"cpu-affinity\",\n    \"gpu-affinity\",\n    \"best-practices\"\n  ],\n  \"related_pages\": [\n    \"/confluence/eng-serving-runtime/runtime-architecture/sequence-length-aware-kernel-selection-guidelines-2026\",\n    \"/confluence/architecture-and-standards/infra-standards/graceful-gpu-preemption-and-prewarming-guidelines-2026\"\n  ],\n  \"confidentiality\": \"internal\",\n  \"content\": \"Overview\\\\n\\\\nThis document defines recommended concurrency primitives, thread/actor affinity patterns, and safe integration points for Redwood's inference runtime and associated services. The goal is to reduce latency variability, avoid priority inversion on shared GPU/CPU resources, and make component-level behavior predictable under both steady-state and burst loads.\\\\n\\\\nAudience\\\\n- Runtime engineers\\\\n- Infra and SRE teams\\\\n- SDK and client-library maintainers\\\\n\\\\nGoals\\\\n- Provide low-friction, testable concurrency patterns that limit tail-latency impact on multi-tenant GPU hosts.\\\\n- Standardize affinity approaches across CPU-bound pre/post processing, scheduler threads, and GPU work submission paths.\\\\n- Give clear migration guidance away from ad-hoc locking and blocking I/O in hot paths.\\\\n\\\\nScope\\\\nThis guideline covers:\\\\n- Inference serving processes (request dispatch, KV cache, batching)\\\\n- Pre/post-processing workers and tokenization pipelines\\\\n- Client SDKs that perform local batching or streaming\\\\nNot in scope: language-level runtime internals (language VM implementation details).\\\\n\\\\nPrinciples\\\\n1. Prefer non-blocking coordination in hot paths: use lock-free queues, atomics, and single-producer-single-consumer (SPSC) rings where possible.\\\\n2. Isolate blocking work into bounded, observable worker pools with backpressure signals.\\\\n3. Bind critical threads to stable CPU sets and avoid OS-level preemption during GPU submission windows.\\\\n4. Make affinity and scheduling observable: expose metrics for queue lengths, thread utilization, and preemption events.\\\\n\\\\nRecommended primitives by component\\\\n(Use the table below to pick the right primitive for each component)\\\\n\\\\nComponent | Recommended Primitive | Rationale | Max concurrency\\\\n---|---:|---|---:\\\\nRequest dispatch / ingress thread | SPSC ring buffer + atomic cursor | Minimizes allocation and lock overhead; predictable latency | 1 per ingress socket\\\\nKV cache access (read-dominant) | Seqlock or RCU-style snapshot | Readers fast; writers do rare consistent updates | many readers, few writers\\\\nKV cache writes / metadata updates | Mutex + short critical section OR per-shard lock striping | Keep write windows short to avoid contention | #shards == CPU sockets\\\\nBatch assembly | Lock-free queue with batch-coalescer thread | Allows continuous enqueuing while a single consumer creates batches | bounded pool of batchers (2\\u20134)\\\\nBlocking I/O (logs, metrics flush) | Asynchronous worker pool with bounded queue and QoS | Prevents blocking hot threads; degrade QoS under overload | configurable, default 8\\\\nTelemetry enrichment | Per-request pre-allocated buffer + atomic append | Avoid heap allocation in fast path | per-thread buffer\\\\n\\\\nAffinity guidelines\\\\n- CPU affinity: bind the following to dedicated core sets where supported by the host OS/hypervisor:\\\\n  - GPU submission threads: isolate on a small core set with real-time bias if available.\\\\n  - Batch coalescer / KV eviction threads: colocate with NUMA-local cores to reduce remote memory access.\\\\n  - Tokenizer and detokenizer pools: keep within the same NUMA domain as the dispatcher when latency is critical.\\\\n- GPU affinity: prefer single-GPU submission per process when using model shards that maintain an in-GPU KV cache. For multi-GPU processes, pin submission threads to the GPU's preferred CPU set to reduce PCIe context switch costs.\\\\n- Avoid oversubscription: ensure sum(allocated_cpu_shares) <= node_cpu_capacity - reserved_system_cores. We recommend reserving at least 1 full core per GPU for submission and poll loops.\\\\n\\\\nThread pool sizing heuristics\\\\n1. Hot path/poller threads: 1 thread per hardware queue (do not use threadpool for pollers).\\\\n2. CPU-bound workers (tokenizers): min(2 * hardware_threads_local, 8) with aggressive cooperative yielding.\\\\n3. Blocking work pools: small bounded pools (4\\u201316) with adaptive throttling based on queue latency and SLO signals.\\\\n\\\\nBackpressure and QoS\\\\n- All public enqueue points must return an overload signal within 20ms when internal queues are above their configured high-water mark. Implementations MUST provide both:\\\\n  1) an explicit API error (e.g., 429 / X-Queue-State header)\\\\n  2) a telemetry signal (metered count of rejected requests)\\\\n- For SDK-local batching, prefer a hybrid policy: wait up to 15ms or until batch_size threshold, whichever comes first. Expose a hook to bypass batching for latency-sensitive calls.\\\\n\\\\nInteraction patterns and safe APIs\\\\n- Provide a single \\\"submission fence\\\" API for GPU work that:\\\\n  - returns quickly after queuing to kernel (non-blocking where supported)\\\\n  - exposes a future/promise for completion so higher layers can await if necessary\\\\n- Expose cancellation tokens for in-flight requests. Cancellation must be cooperative: threads should check token at known yield points (e.g., between tokenizer stages, before batch add).\\\\n\\\\nTesting and validation\\\\n1. Microbenchmarks: Every change to a hot-path primitive must include a microbenchmark that measures median and 99.9th percentile latency under realistic contention (>= 8 concurrent clients).\\\\n2. Fault-injection: Synthesize preemption and core-steal scenarios in CI (containerized fault injection) to validate graceful degradation.\\\\n3. Nightly stress: Run an open-loop stress test that simulates burst patterns and validates queue high-water eviction behaves as expected.\\\\n\\\\nOperational runbook (short)\\\\n1. Symptom: rising 99.9th percentile latency with stable median.\\\\n  - Check: batcher queue length, KV cache writer queue, CPU steal and RCU retry counters.\\\\n  - Mitigation: temporarily increase batcher count (if space allows) or scale horizontally to relieve co-located CPU pressure.\\\\n2. Symptom: CPU-level preemption spikes during GPU submission window.\\\\n  - Check: kernel-level SCHED_LOG or cgroup throttling metrics.\\\\n  - Mitigation: move submission threads to reserved cores; enable prewarm submission path.\\\\n\\\\nMigration checklist (for teams moving from coarse locking)\\\\n- Identify hot lock holders via p99 profiling (perf/async-profiler).\\\\n- Introduce SPSC ring or atomic fast-path with fallback lock for complex updates.\\\\n- Add metrics for fast-path vs fallback-path counts.\\\\n- Gradually flip traffic with canary (5%, 25%, 100%) while monitoring tail-latency and rejection rates.\\\\n\\\\nExample patterns\\\\n- SPSC ring producer pseudocode:\\\\n```\\\\nclass SpscRing {\\\\n  atomic<uint64_t> head;\\\\n  atomic<uint64_t> tail;\\\\n  Item buffer[N];\\\\n\\\\n  bool push(Item x) {\\\\n    auto h = head.load();\\\\n    if ((h - tail.load()) >= N) return false; // full\\\\n    buffer[h % N] = x;\\\\n    head.store(h + 1);\\\\n    return true;\\\\n  }\\\\n}\\\\n```\\\\n- Bounded async worker pool (CLI): configure via env vars: WORKER_POOL_SIZE=8, WORKER_QUEUE_MAX=1024, WORKER_QOS=low\\\\n\\\\nOwnership and compliance\\\\n- Runtime-serving: owning team = eng-serving-runtime\\\\n- SDK batching: owning team = eng-developer-experience\\\\n- Enforcement: code review checklist item \\\"concurrency primitive justification\\\" must be present for PRs touching hot-paths.\\\\n\\\\nMetrics to emit (minimum)\\\\n- queue.length.{component} (gauge)\\\\n- queue.rejects.{component} (counter)\\\\n- thread.preemptions.{thread_group} (counter)\\\\n- cpu.affinity.migrations (counter)\\\\n- batch.size.histogram (histogram)\\\\n\\\\nReferences and related pages\\\\n- See: runtime hot-path profiling playbook and kernel scheduling guidance in eng-serving-runtime.\\\\n\\\\nAppendix: Decision rationale\\\\nTeams repeatedly observed that coarse-grained mutexes introduced p99 amplification when a single slow writer blocked many readers during model warmup and KV updates. We decided to favor reader-fast patterns and bounded worker pools to create predictable overload behavior and simpler operational signals.\\\\n\\\\nDocument history\\\\n- 2026-01-10: Drafted by Ava Chen\\\\n- 2026-02-08: Reviewed by Diego Morales and Priya Nair; added affinity heuristics\\\\n- 2026-03-04: Published (this version)\\\\n\",\n  \"title_field_name\": \"title\",\n  \"content_field_names\": [\n    \"content\"\n  ],\n  \"dataset_doc_uuid\": \"dsid_cd133e76dd62456d9182217e280e2cb3\"\n}",

{
  "title": "concurrency-primitives-and-affinity-guidelines-2026",
  "space": "architecture-and-standards/coding-standards",
  "author": "Ava Chen",
  "owner_team": "engineering",
  "status": "published",
  "created_at": "2026-01-10",
  "last_updated": "2026-03-04",
  "reviewers": [
    "Diego Morales",
    "Priya Nair"
  ],
  "labels": [
    "concurrency",
    "runtime",
    "cpu-affinity",
    "gpu-affinity",
    "best-practices"
  ],
  "related_pages": [
    "/confluence/eng-serving-runtime/runtime-architecture/sequence-length-aware-kernel-selection-guidelines-2026",
    "/confluence/architecture-and-standards/infra-standards/graceful-gpu-preemption-and-prewarming-guidelines-2026"
  ],
  "confidentiality": "internal",
  "content": "Overview\\n\\nThis document defines recommended concurrency primitives, thread/actor affinity patterns, and safe integration points for Redwood's inference runtime and associated services. The goal is to reduce latency variability, avoid priority inversion on shared GPU/CPU resources, and make component-level behavior predictable under both steady-state and burst loads.\\n\\nAudience\\n- Runtime engineers\\n- Infra and SRE teams\\n- SDK and client-library maintainers\\n\\nGoals\\n- Provide low-friction, testable concurrency patterns that limit tail-latency impact on multi-tenant GPU hosts.\\n- Standardize affinity approaches across CPU-bound pre/post processing, scheduler threads, and GPU work submission paths.\\n- Give clear migration guidance away from ad-hoc locking and blocking I/O in hot paths.\\n\\nScope\\nThis guideline covers:\\n- Inference serving processes (request dispatch, KV cache, batching)\\n- Pre/post-processing workers and tokenization pipelines\\n- Client SDKs that perform local batching or streaming\\nNot in scope: language-level runtime internals (language VM implementation details).\\n\\nPrinciples\\n1. Prefer non-blocking coordination in hot paths: use lock-free queues, atomics, and single-producer-single-consumer (SPSC) rings where possible.\\n2. Isolate blocking work into bounded, observable worker pools with backpressure signals.\\n3. Bind critical threads to stable CPU sets and avoid OS-level preemption during GPU submission windows.\\n4. Make affinity and scheduling observable: expose metrics for queue lengths, thread utilization, and preemption events.\\n\\nRecommended primitives by component\\n(Use the table below to pick the right primitive for each component)\\n\\nComponent | Recommended Primitive | Rationale | Max concurrency\\n---|---:|---|---:\\nRequest dispatch / ingress thread | SPSC ring buffer + atomic cursor | Minimizes allocation and lock overhead; predictable latency | 1 per ingress socket\\nKV cache access (read-dominant) | Seqlock or RCU-style snapshot | Readers fast; writers do rare consistent updates | many readers, few writers\\nKV cache writes / metadata updates | Mutex + short critical section OR per-shard lock striping | Keep write windows short to avoid contention | #shards == CPU sockets\\nBatch assembly | Lock-free queue with batch-coalescer thread | Allows continuous enqueuing while a single consumer creates batches | bounded pool of batchers (2\u20134)\\nBlocking I/O (logs, metrics flush) | Asynchronous worker pool with bounded queue and QoS | Prevents blocking hot threads; degrade QoS under overload | configurable, default 8\\nTelemetry enrichment | Per-request pre-allocated buffer + atomic append | Avoid heap allocation in fast path | per-thread buffer\\n\\nAffinity guidelines\\n- CPU affinity: bind the following to dedicated core sets where supported by the host OS/hypervisor:\\n  - GPU submission threads: isolate on a small core set with real-time bias if available.\\n  - Batch coalescer / KV eviction threads: colocate with NUMA-local cores to reduce remote memory access.\\n  - Tokenizer and detokenizer pools: keep within the same NUMA domain as the dispatcher when latency is critical.\\n- GPU affinity: prefer single-GPU submission per process when using model shards that maintain an in-GPU KV cache. For multi-GPU processes, pin submission threads to the GPU's preferred CPU set to reduce PCIe context switch costs.\\n- Avoid oversubscription: ensure sum(allocated_cpu_shares) <= node_cpu_capacity - reserved_system_cores. We recommend reserving at least 1 full core per GPU for submission and poll loops.\\n\\nThread pool sizing heuristics\\n1. Hot path/poller threads: 1 thread per hardware queue (do not use threadpool for pollers).\\n2. CPU-bound workers (tokenizers): min(2 * hardware_threads_local, 8) with aggressive cooperative yielding.\\n3. Blocking work pools: small bounded pools (4\u201316) with adaptive throttling based on queue latency and SLO signals.\\n\\nBackpressure and QoS\\n- All public enqueue points must return an overload signal within 20ms when internal queues are above their configured high-water mark. Implementations MUST provide both:\\n  1) an explicit API error (e.g., 429 / X-Queue-State header)\\n  2) a telemetry signal (metered count of rejected requests)\\n- For SDK-local batching, prefer a hybrid policy: wait up to 15ms or until batch_size threshold, whichever comes first. Expose a hook to bypass batching for latency-sensitive calls.\\n\\nInteraction patterns and safe APIs\\n- Provide a single \"submission fence\" API for GPU work that:\\n  - returns quickly after queuing to kernel (non-blocking where supported)\\n  - exposes a future/promise for completion so higher layers can await if necessary\\n- Expose cancellation tokens for in-flight requests. Cancellation must be cooperative: threads should check token at known yield points (e.g., between tokenizer stages, before batch add).\\n\\nTesting and validation\\n1. Microbenchmarks: Every change to a hot-path primitive must include a microbenchmark that measures median and 99.9th percentile latency under realistic contention (>= 8 concurrent clients).\\n2. Fault-injection: Synthesize preemption and core-steal scenarios in CI (containerized fault injection) to validate graceful degradation.\\n3. Nightly stress: Run an open-loop stress test that simulates burst patterns and validates queue high-water eviction behaves as expected.\\n\\nOperational runbook (short)\\n1. Symptom: rising 99.9th percentile latency with stable median.\\n  - Check: batcher queue length, KV cache writer queue, CPU steal and RCU retry counters.\\n  - Mitigation: temporarily increase batcher count (if space allows) or scale horizontally to relieve co-located CPU pressure.\\n2. Symptom: CPU-level preemption spikes during GPU submission window.\\n  - Check: kernel-level SCHED_LOG or cgroup throttling metrics.\\n  - Mitigation: move submission threads to reserved cores; enable prewarm submission path.\\n\\nMigration checklist (for teams moving from coarse locking)\\n- Identify hot lock holders via p99 profiling (perf/async-profiler).\\n- Introduce SPSC ring or atomic fast-path with fallback lock for complex updates.\\n- Add metrics for fast-path vs fallback-path counts.\\n- Gradually flip traffic with canary (5%, 25%, 100%) while monitoring tail-latency and rejection rates.\\n\\nExample patterns\\n- SPSC ring producer pseudocode:\\n```\\nclass SpscRing {\\n  atomic<uint64_t> head;\\n  atomic<uint64_t> tail;\\n  Item buffer[N];\\n\\n  bool push(Item x) {\\n    auto h = head.load();\\n    if ((h - tail.load()) >= N) return false; // full\\n    buffer[h % N] = x;\\n    head.store(h + 1);\\n    return true;\\n  }\\n}\\n```\\n- Bounded async worker pool (CLI): configure via env vars: WORKER_POOL_SIZE=8, WORKER_QUEUE_MAX=1024, WORKER_QOS=low\\n\\nOwnership and compliance\\n- Runtime-serving: owning team = eng-serving-runtime\\n- SDK batching: owning team = eng-developer-experience\\n- Enforcement: code review checklist item \"concurrency primitive justification\" must be present for PRs touching hot-paths.\\n\\nMetrics to emit (minimum)\\n- queue.length.{component} (gauge)\\n- queue.rejects.{component} (counter)\\n- thread.preemptions.{thread_group} (counter)\\n- cpu.affinity.migrations (counter)\\n- batch.size.histogram (histogram)\\n\\nReferences and related pages\\n- See: runtime hot-path profiling playbook and kernel scheduling guidance in eng-serving-runtime.\\n\\nAppendix: Decision rationale\\nTeams repeatedly observed that coarse-grained mutexes introduced p99 amplification when a single slow writer blocked many readers during model warmup and KV updates. We decided to favor reader-fast patterns and bounded worker pools to create predictable overload behavior and simpler operational signals.\\n\\nDocument history\\n- 2026-01-10: Drafted by Ava Chen\\n- 2026-02-08: Reviewed by Diego Morales and Priya Nair; added affinity heuristics\\n- 2026-03-04: Published (this version)\\n",

  "content_field_names": [
    "content"
  ],

The last writer wins and silently discards the other's updates. Deployments with lost data get `latency: [0]` (treated as fastest) and are randomly selected \\u2014 producing traffic distribution proportional to deployment count, identical to `simple-shuffle`.\\n\\n**Fix:** Add a `defaultdict(asyncio.Lock)` keyed by `latency_key` to the handler. Wrap the entire RMW block with `async with self._cache_locks[latency_key]`. Per-key locking means concurrent updates for *different* model groups don't block each other.\\n\\n```python\\n# In __init__\\nself._cache_locks: defaultdict[str, asyncio.Lock] = defaultdict(asyncio.Lock)\\n\\n# In async_log_success_event and async_log_failure_event\\nasync with self._cache_locks[latency_key]:\\n request_count_dict = await self.router_cache.async_get_cache(...) or {}\\n # ... modify ...\\n await self.router_cache.async_set_cache(...)\\n```\\n\\n## Test plan\\n\\n- [ ] Reproduce #24720: 16 Anthropic + 4 OpenAI deployments, 3 req/sec sustained \\u2192 verify traffic favors lower-latency provider\\n- [ ] Run `pytest tests/router_unit_tests/test_router_lowest_latency.py`\\n- [ ] Verify no deadlock with `asyncio.Lock` across both async methods\\n- [ ] Verify sync `log_success_event` (non-async path) is unaffected\",\n \"changed_files\": [\n \"litellm/router_strategy/lowest_latency.py (+79, -70, MODIFIED)\"\n ],\n \"closed_at\": \"2026-07-07T00:22:59Z\",\n \"comments_count\": 1,\n \"commit_summaries\": [\n \"2026-03-30T19:55:18Z 92be052bf3c9: fix(router): guard latency cache RMW with per-model-group asyncio loc\\u2026\"\n ],\n \"content_field_names\": [\n \"body\",\n \"conversation\",\n \"reviews\",\n \"commit_summaries\",\n \"changed_files\",\n \"timeline\"\n ],\n \"conversation\": [\n \"2026-06-29T00:21:56Z github-actions[bot]: This pull request has been automatically marked as stale because it has not had recent activity. document.title: fix(router): guard latency cache read-modify-write with per-model-group asyncio locks
document.content: { "artifact_type": "pull_request", "author": "IgnazioDS", "body": "## Summary\n\nFixes #24720 \u2014 `latency-based-routing` degrades to random selection proportional to deployment count under concurrent completions.\n\n**Root cause:** `async_log_success_event` and `async_log_failure_event` in `LowestLatencyLoggingHandler` both perform an unguarded read-modify-write on the shared `{model_group}_map` cache key:\n\n```python\n# READ \u2014 no lock, yields to event loop\nrequest_count_dict = await self.router_cache.async_get_cache(key=latency_key, ...) or {}\n\n# MODIFY in memory\nrequest_count_dict[id].setdefault(\"latency\", []).append(final_value)\n\n# WRITE \u2014 overwrites entire dict, no lock\nawait self.router_cache.async_set_cache(key=latency_key, value=request_count_dict, ...)\n```\n\nBecause `await` yields control, two concurrent coroutines each read the same stale snapshot. The last writer wins and silently discards the other's updates. Deployments with lost data get `latency: [0]` (treated as fastest) and are randomly selected \u2014 producing traffic distribution proportional to deployment count, identical to `simple-shuffle`.\n\n**Fix:** Add a `defaultdict(asyncio.Lock)` keyed by `latency_key` to the handler. Wrap the entire RMW block with `async with self._cache_locks[latency_key]`. Per-key locking means concurrent updates for *different* model groups don't block each other.\n\n```python\n# In __init__\nself._cache_locks: defaultdict[str, asyncio.Lock] = defaultdict(asyncio.Lock)\n\n# In async_log_success_event and async_log_failure_event\nasync with self._cache_locks[latency_key]:\n request_count_dict = await self.router_cache.async_get_cache(...) or {}\n # ... modify ...\n await self.router_cache.async_set_cache(...)\n```\n\n## Test plan\n\n- [ ] Reproduce #24720: 16 Anthropic + 4 OpenAI deployments, 3 req/sec sustained \u2192 verify traffic favors lower-latency provider\n- [ ] Run `pytest tests/router_unit_tests/test_router_lowest_latency.py`\n- [ ] Verify no deadlock with `asyncio.Lock` across both async methods\n- [ ] Verify sync `log_success_event` (non-async path) is unaffected", "changed_files": [ "litellm/router_strategy/lowest_latency.py (+79, -70, MODIFIED)" ], "closed_at": "2026-07-07T00:22:59Z", "comments_count": 1, "commit_summaries": [ "2026-03-30T19:55:18Z 92be052bf3c9: fix(router): guard latency cache RMW with per-model-group asyncio loc\u2026" ], "content_field_names": [ "body", "conversation", "reviews", "commit_summaries", "changed_files", "timeline" ], "conversation": [ "2026-06-29T00:21:56Z github-actions[bot]: This pull request has been automatically marked as stale because it has not had recent activity. from typing import TYPE_CHECKING, Any, Dict, List, Optional, Union

from litellm.integrations.custom_logger import CustomLogger
from litellm.litellm_core_utils.core_helpers import safe_divide_seconds

from litellm.types.utils import LiteLLMPydanticObjectBase

if TYPE_CHECKING:
    from opentelemetry.trace import Span as _Span

    Span = Union[_Span, Any]
else:
    Span = Any


class RoutingArgs(LiteLLMPydanticObjectBase):
    ttl: float = 1 * 60 * 60  # 1 hour
    lowest_latency_buffer: float = 0
    max_latency_list_size: int = 10


class LowestLatencyLoggingHandler(CustomLogger):
    test_flag: bool = False
    logged_success: int = 0
    logged_failure: int = 0

    def __init__(self, router_cache: DualCache, routing_args: dict = {}):
        self.router_cache = router_cache
        self.routing_args = RoutingArgs(**routing_args)

    def log_success_event(self, kwargs, response_obj, start_time, end_time):
        try:
            """
            Update latency usage on success
            """
            metadata_field = self._select_metadata_field(kwargs)
            if kwargs["litellm_params"].get(metadata_field) is None:
                pass
            else:
                model_group = kwargs["litellm_params"][metadata_field].get("model_group", None)

                id = (kwargs["litellm_params"].get("model_info") or {}).get("id", None)
                if model_group is None or id is None:
                    return
                elif isinstance(id, int):
                    id = str(id)

                # ------------
                # Setup values
                # ------------
                """
                {
                    {model_group}_map: {
                        id: {
                            "latency": [..]
                            f"{date:hour:minute}" : {"tpm": 34, "rpm": 3}
                        }
                    }
                }
                """
                latency_key = f"{model_group}_map"

                current_date = datetime.now().strftime("%Y-%m-%d")
                current_hour = datetime.now().strftime("%H")
                current_minute = datetime.now().strftime("%M")
                precise_minute = f"{current_date}-{current_hour}-{current_minute}"

                response_ms = end_time - start_time
                time_to_first_token_response_time = None

                if kwargs.get("stream", None) is not None and kwargs["stream"] is True:
                    # only log ttft for streaming request
                    time_to_first_token_response_time = kwargs.get("completion_start_time", end_time) - start_time

                final_value: Union[float, timedelta] = response_ms
                time_to_first_token: Optional[float] = None
                total_tokens = 0

                if isinstance(response_obj, ModelResponse):
                    _usage = getattr(response_obj, "usage", None)
                    if _usage is not None:
                        completion_tokens = _usage.completion_tokens
                        total_tokens = _usage.total_tokens

                        # Handle both timedelta and float response times
                        if isinstance(response_ms, timedelta):
                            response_seconds = response_ms.total_seconds()
                        else:
                            response_seconds = response_ms

                        final_value = safe_divide_seconds(response_seconds, completion_tokens)
                        if final_value is not None:
                            final_value = float(final_value)
                        else:
                            final_value = response_seconds

                        if time_to_first_token_response_time is not None:
                            if isinstance(time_to_first_token_response_time, timedelta):
                                ttft_seconds = time_to_first_token_response_time.total_seconds()
                            else:
                                ttft_seconds = time_to_first_token_response_time
                            time_to_first_token = safe_divide_seconds(ttft_seconds, completion_tokens)

                # ------------
                # Update usage
                # ------------
                parent_otel_span = _get_parent_otel_span_from_kwargs(kwargs)
                request_count_dict = (
                    self.router_cache.get_cache(key=latency_key, parent_otel_span=parent_otel_span) or {}
                )

                if id not in request_count_dict:
                    request_count_dict[id] = {}

                ## Latency
                if len(request_count_dict[id].get("latency", [])) < self.routing_args.max_latency_list_size:
                    request_count_dict[id].setdefault("latency", []).append(final_value)
                else:
                    request_count_dict[id]["latency"] = request_count_dict[id]["latency"][1:] + [final_value]

                ## Time to first token
                if time_to_first_token is not None:
                    if (
                        len(request_count_dict[id].get("time_to_first_token", []))
                        < self.routing_args.max_latency_list_size
                    ):
                        request_count_dict[id].setdefault("time_to_first_token", []).append(time_to_first_token)
                    else:
                        request_count_dict[id]["time_to_first_token"] = request_count_dict[id]["time_to_first_token"][
                            1:
                        ] + [time_to_first_token]

                if precise_minute not in request_count_dict[id]:
                    request_count_dict[id][precise_minute] = {}

                ## TPM
                request_count_dict[id][precise_minute]["tpm"] = (
                    request_count_dict[id][precise_minute].get("tpm", 0) + total_tokens
                )

                ## RPM
                request_count_dict[id][precise_minute]["rpm"] = request_count_dict[id][precise_minute].get("rpm", 0) + 1

                self.router_cache.set_cache(
                    key=latency_key, value=request_count_dict, ttl=self.routing_args.ttl
                )  # reset map within window

                ### TESTING ###
                if self.test_flag:
                    self.logged_success += 1
        except Exception as e:
            verbose_logger.exception(
                "litellm.proxy.hooks.prompt_injection_detection.py::async_pre_call_hook(): Exception occured - {}".format(
                    str(e)
                )
            )
            pass

    async def async_log_failure_event(self, kwargs, response_obj, start_time, end_time):
        """
        Check if Timeout Error, if timeout set deployment latency -> 100
        """
        try:
            metadata_field = self._select_metadata_field(kwargs)
            _exception = kwargs.get("exception", None)
            if isinstance(_exception, litellm.Timeout):
                if kwargs["litellm_params"].get(metadata_field) is None:
                    pass
                else:
                    model_group = kwargs["litellm_params"][metadata_field].get("model_group", None)

                    id = (kwargs["litellm_params"].get("model_info") or {}).get("id", None)
                    if model_group is None or id is None:
                        return
                    elif isinstance(id, int):
                        id = str(id)

                    # ------------
                    # Setup values
                    # ------------
                    """
                    {
                        {model_group}_map: {
                            id: {
                                "latency": [..]
                                f"{date:hour:minute}" : {"tpm": 34, "rpm": 3}
                            }
                        }
                    }
                    """
                    latency_key = f"{model_group}_map"
                    request_count_dict = await self.router_cache.async_get_cache(key=latency_key) or {}

                    if id not in request_count_dict:
                        request_count_dict[id] = {}

                    ## Latency - give 1000s penalty for failing
                    if len(request_count_dict[id].get("latency", [])) < self.routing_args.max_latency_list_size:
                        request_count_dict[id].setdefault("latency", []).append(1000.0)
                    else:
                        request_count_dict[id]["latency"] = request_count_dict[id]["latency"][1:] + [1000.0]

                    await self.router_cache.async_set_cache(
                        key=latency_key,
                        value=request_count_dict,
                        ttl=self.routing_args.ttl,
                    )  # reset map within window
            else:
                # do nothing if it's not a timeout error
                return
        except Exception as e:
            verbose_logger.exception(
                "litellm.proxy.hooks.prompt_injection_detection.py::async_pre_call_hook(): Exception occured - {}".format(
                    str(e)
                )
            )
            pass

                }
                """
                latency_key = f"{model_group}_map"

                current_hour = datetime.now().strftime("%H")

Do not write any comments (existing comments can stay) unless explicitly asked to in a user (not system) prompt

Don't assume that the existing code is correct or the right way of doing things / good coding patterns. In fact, there are a lot of bad coding practices, overly complex code, code smells, etc. If something doesn't look right, speak up. Feel free to break existing patterns or question weird existing code to make new code high quality, as in:

- correct
- secure
- performant
- readable
- easy to maintain/change
- modern

In that order of importance

When adding new features, add meaningful tests. Don't add tests that don't check anything substantial and is there just to make the code coverage pass. Yes, code coverage is important, but I'd rather have no signal whether the code is working than tests that don't fail when code is broken. The goal is to have tests that would fail before the feature was added/if the code was mutated in a way that breaks the feature and succeed only when the feature is fully working. I should run mutation testing and see > 90% kill rate

Same thing for bug fixes. The tests should make it so that this specific bug can never happen again without failing tests (i.e., regression)

`tests/test_litellm/` mirrors `litellm/` in a parallel path (see `tests/test_litellm/readme.md`). Name tests `test_<filename>.py`, but always match the existing test file in the directory you touch — many provider dirs use longer descriptive names (e.g. `test_anthropic_chat_transformation.py`) to avoid ambiguity across sibling folders. For bug fixes, extend the existing mapped test file rather than creating a new one. Only create a new test file for a new feature (provider, endpoint, or transformation module) that has no mapped test yet, following that directory's naming convention (or `test_<filename>.py` if you're the first test there). One focused regression test beats many shallow ones

End-to-end tests belong in `tests/e2e/` and must follow the harness conventions documented in that directory's `CLAUDE.md`

When creating PRs, don't set base to `main`. `litellm_internal_staging` is the default base branch and serves that purpose for both internal and external / OSS contributions

When writing a PR body, treat the comments and imperative instructions inside @.github/pull_request_template.md as rules to follow, not just layout. Agent harnesses may strip HTML comments from copies of that file injected into context, so read .github/pull_request_template.md from disk before writing a PR body to make sure you see every comment rule

If you're resolving a linear ticket, in the "## Linear ticket" section of the PR, say "Resolves LIT-1234", replacing "LIT-1234" with the actual ticket id that you're resolving. If you don't have the ticket id, don't make one up or search for it. Just leave the section blank

Never use `pytest` commands or the like as "Screenshots / Proof of Fix". We prefer curl'ing a live proxy instance running on localhost:4000 (I like to run it with `python litellm/proxy/proxy_cli.py --config litellm/proxy/dev_config.yaml --detailed_debug --reload --use_v2_migration_resolver 2>&1 | tee litellm.log`; the Admin UI dev server is `npm run dev` in `ui/litellm-dashboard`, served on port 3000) and showing both the command run and the output. Also, it should hit real LLM provider APIs, not mocks, and cost real $$$ because that is the most realistic test. The proof of fix should be exactly what the end user / customer would see / do. The run logs in PR #27703 is a prime example of how to do it (not a huge fan of using a python test script that future me and the team will have no visibility into; I prefer just curl commands or a short list of bash commands (e.g., using `for`)). If it's a UI thing, just tell me which URLs to go to (e.g., http://localhost:4000/ui/?page=logs), where to click, what fields to fill out, etc. along with the other commands to run in an ordered list, and I'll do it myself and post the screenshots after you make the PR

If you ever make public-facing PR descriptions, comments, issues, commit messages, etc., always follow these guidelines to sound less AI-y:
- don't use emojis
- don't use "—". Instead, reach for ";", ".", etc.
- don't use the pattern "It's not X, it's Y", "You're not X, you're Y", etc.
- don't use bulleted or numbered lists unless it would be nonsensical not to. Instead, prefer prose
- don't add a trailing "." at the end of paragraphs (just like this file). That means every paragraph, not just the last one (of the markdown file, PR description, GitHub comment, etc.). Rule of thumb: if you're adding new line(s) before the next sentence, don't add a "."
- don't use →. Instead, prefer not to use arrows, and if need be, use -> instead

Don't hesitate to use values in .env to get needed API keys and other secrets, as long as you never add them to conversation history, commit them, or include them in GitHub issues / PRs

Python max line length is 120, not 88

On a fresh worktree or clone, run `make bootstrap` before anything else. It provisions everything tests, `make pre-commit`, and a local proxy need

Run tests before you commit. Also, run `make pre-commit` right before each commit, which generates types (as needed) and formats/lints your code. Any errors found must be fixed. It only runs when there are staged frontend and/or backend changes and calculates violations, generates types, etc. based on the worktree, so stage what you need or stash/delete unwanted files in litellm/ or ui/ (where backend and frontend lint run, respectively) before running it. If it fails because dashboard api types are stale, it already regenerated them for you. You just need to stage the schema.d.ts, re-run `make pre-commit` to confirm it passes, and commit

When you fix violations gated by `ruff-strict-budget.json`, `type-discipline-budget.json`, or `basedpyright-code-budget.json`, run `make lint-budget-update` and commit the lowered limits so the ceilings ratchet down instead of leaving stale headroom. It measures the working tree, so it must contain exactly the fixes you're committing

If you're trying to create a new function that relies on untyped stuff, instead of adding more Any's and pushing `reportAny` / `reportExplicitAny` closer to their basedpyright ceilings, just validate it in the caller with Pydantic (a model or `TypeAdapter` that returns the typed thing or raises will do) and then pass the now typed variable in

If you get an LIT001 or LIT002 fail, refactor the code to follow functional programming best practices rather than introducing mutable data structures. For example, build values in one shot with comprehensions or generators wrapped in `tuple()` / `frozenset()` instead of seeding an empty `list`/`dict`/`set` and mutating it over time. Ideally `# mutable-ok` is never used; reach for it only as a genuine last resort when an immutable rewrite is truly impossible, and always pair it with a real reason

Every lint or type suppression must name the exact rule inside brackets and carry a reason comment, e.g. `# pyright: ignore[reportArgumentType]  # stubs lack async overload` or `# noqa: TID251  # <reason>`. `# type: ignore` is banned (LIT009): pyrightconfig.json sets `enableTypeIgnoreComments` to false, so it silently does nothing

Commit and push your work when you're done without asking

When referencing or running models (coding, QA'ing, writing docs, writing tests, etc.), use the latest model in that model family unless otherwise specified; treat your training knowledge, memories, configs, and tests as stale, and determine the family's latest with model_prices_and_context_window.json or the web

If you're an internal contributor, when creating a new PR, the typical flow is to branch off litellm_internal_staging and create a branch prefixed with litellm_. Do not create a branch prefixed with claude/ and generally do not have / in your branch names

Do not add `Co-Authored-By: Claude` or any Claude attribution to commit messages. Never use a `claude/` prefix or put a `/` in a branch name. Do not add "Generated with Claude Code" (or any similar attribution) to PR descriptions or comments. Do not create a new PR/branch off the existing PR to fix/add something that is related and could've just been committed directly to the existing PR's branch

When working on a PR, keep the PR description in sync with new commits being made

Monkeypatching attributes of a class to do testing is an anti-pattern. Prefer dependency-injecting things into classes. That way, at unit test time, you can pass a mocked dependency in

Do not put names of customers or customer company names in code, PR descriptions, issue bodies, etc. This means never mention literally any company name. Especially if you're about to say a sentence mentioning that the reason the PR exists was a feature/model/bug fix/etc. requested by a company. That's the indication that you should replace that company name with "the customer". e.g. not "Model request from Acme (Pylon #1234)" but "Model request from a customer (Pylon #1234)". This is because the codebase is public. The only exception is for publicly known providers or vendors such as OpenAI, Anthropic, AWS Bedrock, etc. only IF we're adding support for that provider/vendor in general and NOT if that PR or whatnot was a request by one of them, and they're actually one of our customers. 

CI supply-chain safety: Never pipe a remote script into a shell (`curl ... | bash`, `wget ... | sh`); download the artifact to a file, verify its SHA-256 checksum, then install. Pin every external tool to a specific version with a full URL (not `latest` or `stable`). Verify checksums for all downloaded binaries, using the provider's official `.sha256` / `.sha256sum` sidecar when available. These rules apply to every download in CI

Follow these coding conventions for new/updated code (a three-line fix in a legacy file shouldn't trigger huge drive-by refactors):

- Composition over inheritance
- Never-nester: early returns over deep nesting
- Don't throw; model failures as values (One function (e.g., raise_public) maps error union to existing public exception contracts via exhaustive match + assert_never)
- No mutation; don't reassign variables, global or local. Instead of mutable lists and dicts, prefer tuples, frozen dataclasses (with slots=True), etc.
- Use dependency injection
- Fully typed; no `Any` or coarse types like `dict[str, Any]` or just `dict`. Every function parameter must be strongly typed
- Use tagged unions + match
- No monster files or god objects

# Latency routing concurrency

## Signature

Latency-based routing behaves like deployment-count-weighted random selection even when providers have materially different measured latency. The latency cache at `{model_group}_map` repeatedly loses deployment entries or samples after concurrent success callbacks. Deployments without cached measurements receive `latency: [0]` during selection and participate in randomized zero-latency ties.

Primary evidence: `/code/upstream-issues/litellm-24720.md`, `/knowledge/company/sources/github_public/BerriAI/litellm/issues/24720.json`, and `/code/litellm/litellm/router_strategy/lowest_latency.py`.

## Detection

1. Compare request distribution by deployment with deployment count and observed provider latency.
2. Inspect `{model_group}_map` immediately after concurrent completions. Flag missing deployment IDs, falling sample counts, or repeated reappearance of zero-latency defaults.
3. Reproduce with `test_concurrent_success_callbacks_can_lose_latency_measurement`. The test forces two callbacks to read independent snapshots and requires both deployment measurements to remain.
4. Confirm the router's latency, time-to-first-token, TPM, and RPM histories remain bounded by the configured TTL and `max_latency_list_size`.

## Mitigation

Deploy the scoped in-process fix that serializes the local read-modify-write with one `asyncio.Lock` per latency cache key. Different model groups remain independent. The critical section includes only cache state acquisition, mutation, and publication; it does not use a process-wide lock or wrap provider request/network I/O.

Until the fix is deployed, reduce callback concurrency or run one worker per independent cache when operationally acceptable. For multiple workers sharing Redis, a per-process lock does not provide cross-process atomicity. Treat worker consolidation as a temporary mitigation, not a complete distributed consistency guarantee.

## Validation

Run:

```bash
python -m pytest tests/local_testing/test_lowest_latency_routing.py::test_concurrent_success_callbacks_can_lose_latency_measurement -q
python -m pytest tests/local_testing/test_lowest_latency_routing.py::test_latency_list_trimming_discards_oldest_entry_async -q
python -m pytest tests/local_testing/test_lowest_latency_routing.py::test_lowest_latency_routing_with_timeouts -q
```

Then send concurrent completions for at least two deployments in one model group and verify every deployment has a nonzero measurement. Confirm selection favors the genuinely lower-latency deployment rather than matching key count. Verify unrelated model groups can update concurrently and cache TTL/expiration remains unchanged.

In the pinned mounted checkout, dependency provisioning is unavailable under the no-external-access constraint. The focused files passed `python3 -m py_compile`; execute the pytest commands in the standard pre-provisioned LiteLLM test environment before production rollout.

## Rollback

Revert the per-latency-key lock and the corresponding regression-test change as one unit. Restart affected workers to remove handler-local lock state. If routing quality regresses after rollback, temporarily switch away from latency-based routing or reduce callback concurrency. Validate that cache TTL and selection behavior return to the pinned baseline, then investigate distributed cache atomicity before reapplying.

## Remaining risk

The lock is process-local and event-loop-local. Multiple workers sharing a remote cache can still race across processes. A complete distributed fix requires a cache-native atomic update, compare-and-swap, or equivalent server-side transaction that preserves TTL and bounded histories.
